title-group.article-title: The exacerbating effects of stable pulmonary tuberculosis on the deterioration of inflammatory response, coagulation function, and pulmonary function in COPD: A propensity score-matched retrospective study

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and tuberculosis pose significant public health challenges, particularly in tuberculosis-endemic developing regions where their co-prevalence may exacerbate the disease burden of chronic airflow obstruction. This study aimed to investigate the impact of stable pulmonary tuberculosis on inflammatory status, coagulation function, and pulmonary function in COPD patients during acute exacerbations.We conducted a retrospective analysis of 68 COPD patients with acute exacerbation and stable pulmonary tuberculosis (observation group) admitted between December 2019 and December 2023. Using propensity score matching based on age and gender, we selected 68 COPD patients without stable pulmonary tuberculosis as the control group. Comparative analysis of laboratory tests and pulmonary function parameters revealed that the observation group had significantly elevated levels of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), interleukin-6 (IL-6), lymphocyte count, platelet count (PLT), and D-dimer, along with significantly reduced pulmonary function parameters including forced expiratory volume in 1 s/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) and forced expiratory flow between 25 %-75 % of vital capacity (FEF25-FEF75) (all P < 0.05). Correlation analysis demonstrated positive associations between ESR/IL-6 levels and D-dimer, PLT, and fibrin(ogen) degradation product (FDP) levels (P < 0.05).Binary logistic regression analysis of 14 significantly different variables identified IL-6 (OR = 1.056), ESR (OR = 1.022), PLT (OR = 1.005), D-Dimer (OR = 1.002), FEV1/FVC (OR = 0.962), FEF50 (OR = 0.534), and FEF75 (OR = 0.089) as independent factors associated with acute exacerbation in COPD patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis (all P < 0.05). Our findings indicate that elevated IL-6, ESR, PLT, and D-Dimer levels coupled with decreased FEV1/FVC, FEF50, and FEF75 levels represent distinctive clinical characteristics of these patients.This study demonstrates that COPD patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis exhibit enhanced inflammatory responses, prothrombotic tendencies, and more severe pulmonary function impairment, providing a scientific basis for developing individualized treatment strategies for this patient population.

sec.p: Keywords: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, Pulmonary Tuberculosis Respiratory Function, Inflammatory Response, Blood Coagulation
Collection date 2025 Aug.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a major global health concern, affecting an estimated 6 % to 20 % of the world's population and ranking as the third leading cause of death worldwide. While smoking and dust exposure have long been established as the main risk factors for COPD, recent research has increasingly focused on the role of respiratory infections, particularly tuberculosis, in the progression of the disease。A significant proportion of COPD patients—22.6 %—report a history of TB, and nearly half display signs of past TB on CT imaging [1].Post-treatment, lung function in TB patients is likely to deteriorate further, potentially at a more accelerated rate than in individuals without prior tuberculosis infection. Patients with prior tuberculosis infection frequently exhibit more severe respiratory symptoms, a higher frequency of acute exacerbations, and a poor response to the standard treatment for COPD—bronchodilators. However, the specific impact of prior tuberculosis infection on the clinical manifestations and therapeutic responsiveness in COPD patients remain unclear. This study aims to investigate the potential impact of stable pulmonary tuberculosis on inflammatory status, coagulation function, and pulmonary function in COPD patients by comparing those with and without stable tuberculosis. The findings will provide a theoretical basis for developing individualized treatment strategies for COPD patients with concomitant stable tuberculosis, potentially improving their quality of life and prognosis.

sec.title: Study population and study design
sec.p: This study adopted a retrospective cohort design, collecting data from patients hospitalized at the Respiratory Center of the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University between December 2019 and December 2023, with a primary discharge diagnosis of acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (ICD-10 codes: J44.900/J44.100/J44.000).

sec.title: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sec.p: Inclusion Criteria:The diagnostic criteria for COPD patients refer to the standards set by the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) 2019 revised edition [2].The diagnostic criteria for COPD patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis: Refer to the diagnostic criteria in WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis [3].

Exclusion Criteria: (a) The diagnostic criteria for excluding active tuberculosis refer to the NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) guidelines on the diagnosis and prevention of tuberculosis [4]. (b) Exclude hematologic diseases and autoimmune diseases that significantly affect the immune system. (c) Exclude other pulmonary diseases that severely impair lung function, such as bronchiectasis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. (d) Exclude diseases affecting coagulation function, such as pulmonary embolism. (e) Exclude cases with incomplete data collection.(f) Exclude patients with indeterminate results on the tuberculosis-specific interferon-gamma release assay (TB-IGRA).

Grouping Criteria: (a) Observation Group: Patients with a clear history of tuberculosis diagnosis and treatment, having completed anti-tuberculosis therapy; Chest CT imaging showing evidence of stable tuberculous lesions; Meeting the diagnostic criteria for COPD while also fulfilling the diagnostic criteria for inactive tuberculosis; Positive for the tuberculosis-specific interferon-gamma release assay (TB-IGRA) (b) Control Group: No documented history of tuberculosis diagnosis or treatment;Chest CT imaging showing no evidence of old/inactive tuberculous lesions; Meeting the diagnostic criteria for COPD; Negative for the tuberculosis-specific interferon-gamma release assay (TB-IGRA).

sec.title: Research Methods
sec.p: Clinical data from all patient groups upon initial admission prior to treatment (including age, gender, and length of hospital stay) were collected for this retrospective study. A standardized blood collection protocol was implemented for all relevant indicators: On the day of admission, 10 mL of whole blood was obtained via venipuncture using vacuum blood collection tubes containing anticoagulant. The samples were centrifuged at 3500 rpm for 15 min to separate components, after which serum and plasma fractions were immediately aliquoted and stored at −20 °C in an ultra-low temperature environment. This preservation method ensured the stability of bioactive substances to support subsequent testing requirements.

list-item.label: (I)
list-item.p: Laboratory test results: (a) Hematological parameters: Standardized testing was performed using a Hitachi LABOSPECT 008AS fully automated biochemical analyzer to determine complete blood counts (including neutrophils, eosinophils, and lymphocytes) and platelet parameters (count and mean platelet volume), with calculation of the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR). (b) Thrombosis and coagulation parameters: Plasma concentrations of D-dimer and fibrinogen degradation products (FDP) were quantitatively measured using a CFMS LEPU-8800 TEG coagulation analyzer. (c) Inflammatory markers: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was measured in serum using the Westergren method, while C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels were determined by fully automated immunoturbidimetric assay using reagents provided by Beckman Coulter (USA).

sec.p: TB-IGRA (Tuberculosis-specific Interferon-Gamma Release Assay): The TB-IGRA is an advanced immunological assay used to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) infection by measuring T-cell immune responses. Unlike traditional tuberculin skin tests (TST), T-IGRA is highly specific and unaffected by prior BCG vaccination or most non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM).The TB-IGRA test reagent was provided by Beijing Wantai Company. For all patients, 4 mL of heparin anticoagulant blood was collected, and within 2 h, the whole blood sample was mixed by inverting 3 to 5 times, then 1 mL was aliquoted into a background control culture tube (N), a test culture tube (T), and a positive control culture tube (P), mixed, and incubated at 37 °C for 22 ± 2 h. After centrifugation at 3000–5000 r/min for 10 min, the supernatant of each tube was tested using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The optical density values obtained after the test were substituted into the standard curve to calculate the corresponding plasma IFN-γ content. (a) Criteria for positive T-cell interferon-gamma release assay:The negative control value (IGRA-N) must be < 8.0 IU/mL. The positive control value (IGRA-P) must be > 0.5 IU/mL.The difference between the IFN-γ released by MTB-specific CD4 + T cells (IGRA-T) and the negative control (IGRA-N) must be ≥ 0.35 IU/mL to be considered positive; otherwise, the result is negative. (b) Interpretation of indeterminate TB-IGRA results: The negative control value (IGRA-N) is > 8.0 IU/mL, or the positive control value (IGRA-P) is < 0.5 IU/mL.

Pulmonary function test: Professional technicians in our hospital's pulmonary function laboratory used a Jaeger pulmonary function testing instrument produced by Jaeger Company, Germany, to measure the pulmonary ventilation function indicators of each group of patients. The subjects first underwent baseline pulmonary function tests. Subsequently, they inhaled the β2-agonist salbutamol (400 μg) via a metered-dose inhaler (MDI). Fifteen minutes after inhaling salbutamol, the pulmonary function was retested three times, and the best value was recorded. The measured indicators included: forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), FEV1 as a percentage of the predicted value, FEV1/FVC ratio, and forced expiratory flow at 25 % (FEF25), 50 % (FEF50), and 75 % of vital capacity (FEF75).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data were processed and analyzed using the SPSS 25.0 statistical software. When the measurement data were normally distributed, they were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (mean ± SD), and t-tests or analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used. When the measurement data were not normally distributed, they were expressed as median (interquartile range) [M (Q1, Q3)], and non-parametric rank sum tests were used. The level of significance was set at α = 0.05, and P < 0.05 was considered to indicate a statistically significant difference. Correlation analysis was performed using univariate regression analysis, with P < 0.05 considered to indicate a statistically significant difference.

sec.title: Baseline characteristics of participants
sec.p: This study conducted a comprehensive review of discharge diagnoses within our hospital's respiratory department's medical record system from January 2020 to December 2023, identifying 1,462 cases with COPD as the primary diagnosis. Upon rigorous application of our inclusion and exclusion criteria, a total of 168 COPD patients were meticulously selected for the study, ensuring the robustness of our findings. The patient enrollment process is clearly outlined in Fig. 1.

caption.p: Cohort identification and case-control matching are used for preliminary analysis.IPF:Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis.

sec.p: Among the enrolled participants, 77 were male and 91 were female, with an average age of 69.58 years, encompassing a broad age spectrum from 38 to 90 years old. The study was structured to include an observation group of 83 cases and a control group of 85 cases. A significant age disparity was observed between the groups, with the observation group exhibiting a lower average age (P < 0.05), highlighting a critical demographic distinction that has been appropriately accounted for in our analysis.

To control for potential confounding effects of age, gender, smoking status, and comorbidities on laboratory test results and pulmonary function parameters, we employed propensity score matching (with a caliper width set at 0.025) using patient age and gender as matching variables. Through this rigorous matching process, we successfully identified 68 COPD patients with confirmed stable pulmonary tuberculosis as the observation group and precisely matched them with 68 COPD patients without tuberculosis infection as the control group. After matching, there were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in terms of age, gender, smoking status, or comorbidities (see Table 1).

caption.p: General Conditions of the Observation Group and the Control Group.

sec.title: Comparison of Routine blood test results
sec.p: The COPD group with stable pulmonary tuberculosis demonstrated significantly elevated levels of ESR, PLT, IL-6, D-Dimer, and lymphocyte count, which were all statistically higher than those observed in the COPD group without stable pulmonary tuberculosis, as depicted in Fig. 2 A-E (P < 0.05). However, the levels of neutrophils, white blood cells, eosinophils, CRP, MPV, FDP, and PLR did not show statistically significant differences between the two groups, as detailed in Table 2 (P > 0.05).

sec.title: Comparison of pulmonary function indicators
sec.p: Patients with COPD and stable pulmonary tuberculosis showed reduced pulmonary function, with significantly lower values in indicators such as FEV1/FVC, FEF25, FEF50, and FEF75, when compared to those with COPD alone (as illustrated in Fig. 2 F-I). These differences were statistically significant (P < 0.05). In contrast, no significant variations were observed in FEV1, FVC, and FEV1% predicted between the groups with and without stable pulmonary tuberculosis (P > 0.05), as detailed in Table 3.

sec.title: Results of the binary logistic regression analysis
sec.p: In our study, eight clinical features with significant differences (P < 0.05) in the univariate analysis (IL-6, ESR, PLT, D-Dimer, FEV1/FVC, FEF50, and FEF75) were included in the binary logistic regression model. The binary logistic regression revealed that IL-6 (OR = 1.056), ESR (OR = 1.022), PLT (OR = 1.005), D-Dimer (OR = 1.002), FEV1/FVC (OR = 0.962), FEF50 (OR = 0.534), and FEF75 (OR = 0.089) were independently associated with AECOPD in patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis. These results suggest that patients with elevated levels of IL-6, ESR, PLT, and D-Dimer, as well as reduced levels of FEV1/FVC, FEF50, and FEF75, are at a higher risk of AECOPD with stable pulmonary tuberculosis (Table 4).

caption.p: Binary logistic regression analysis of independent factors associated with a history of tuberculosis.

sec.title: Correlation analysis between inflammatory markers and coagulation
sec.p: Univariate regression analysis revealed a positive correlation between IL and 6 levels and blood D-dimer levels (r = 0.339, P < 0.05) (Fig. 4 C), and between ESR levels and blood D-dimer levels (r = 0.232, P < 0.05) (Fig. 4 A). Additionally, there was a positive correlation between ESR levels and platelet count (PLT) (r = 0.351, P < 0.05) (Fig. 4 B), and between IL and 6 levels and fibrin/fibrinogen degradation products (FDP) levels (r = 0.273, P < 0.05) (Fig. 4 D). There was no correlation between IL and 6 levels and platelet count (PLT) (P > 0.05), nor between ESR levels and FDP levels (P > 0.05) (Table 5, Fig. 3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study represents a paradigm shift from previous research focused on active pulmonary tuberculosis, pioneering the investigation into the sustained impact of stable pulmonary tuberculosis on the clinical progression of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Although standardized treatment can achieve “clinical cure” for pulmonary tuberculosis, the irreversible lung tissue damage still leads to post-tuberculosis lung disease (PTLD) [5], a condition recognized since 2019 by the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) as a significant risk factor for COPD development [6].

Our research aims to elucidate the potential effects of stable pulmonary tuberculosis on inflammatory status, coagulation function, and pulmonary function in COPD patients during acute exacerbations. Through this retrospective study, we provide possible insights into the persistent detrimental effects of tuberculosis infection on lung health and its underlying mechanisms in exacerbating COPD. These findings establish a crucial theoretical foundation for developing personalized treatment strategies for COPD patients with comorbid stable pulmonary tuberculosis.

Airflow limitation is a hallmark feature of COPD. This study found that COPD patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis exhibited more significant declines in FEV1/FVC, along with lower FEF50% and FEF75% (indicators reflecting small airway function) compared to the control group, while no significant difference was observed in FVC between the two groups. These findings suggest that prior tuberculosis infection exacerbates pulmonary function impairment in COPD patients, including damage to small airways. Our previous study [7] demonstrated that persistent stimulation of macrophages by ESAT-6, a secretory protein of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, can induce apoptosis in M1-type macrophages. This process compromises the innate immune defense of the airways, thereby increasing susceptibility to respiratory infections. Singh's study [8] similarly identified an association between macrophage phagocytic dysfunction and increased frequency of acute exacerbations in COPD patients. Therefore, tuberculosis infection may contribute to impaired macrophage phagocytic function [9], which could represent one mechanism by which stable pulmonary tuberculosis exacerbates COPD-related pulmonary dysfunction. Building upon these preliminary findings, we plan to conduct further research on macrophage phagocytic function in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid from COPD patients with stable tuberculosis to validate these results. In addition, fibrosis of lung tissue in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis can lead to local bronchiectasis, narrowing of small bronchi, and even atrophy of the affected lung lobes [10]. These pathological changes further impair airway ventilation function, resulting in progressive pulmonary function decline and frequent acute exacerbations. Rhee et al. [11] pointed out that tuberculosis leads to mixed pulmonary ventilation disorders, with FVC, VC, TLC, and FEV1/FVC)% all being lower than in COPD patients without a history of tuberculosis.

Furthermore, our study found no significant differences in age or gender distribution between the two patient groups. Notably, the group with stable pulmonary tuberculosis had a lower mean age. Stable pulmonary tuberculosis can lead to pulmonary function impairment and earlier onset of airway obstruction, resulting in these patients developing COPD at a younger age − a distinguishing characteristic compared to smoking-induced COPD patients. Typically, smoking-related COPD shows a higher prevalence in males. However, our findings suggest that stable pulmonary tuberculosis infection may attenuate gender differences in COPD development.

This study discovered that COPD patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis exhibit a more significant increase in ESR and IL-6 compared to those with COPD alone, aligning with findings from the literature [12]. It has been established that the inflammatory response is pivotal throughout the entire progression of COPD, affecting at least 70 % of patients who experience an elevation in at least one inflammatory marker. During the early stages of COPD, inflammatory mediators are released, drawing neutrophils to the bronchial submucosa, where they further release proteolytic enzymes and reactive oxygen species, mediating bronchial remodeling, leading to airflow limitation, and hastening the advancement of COPD [13]. During acute exacerbations, there is a notable increase in ESR, CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α [14]. Furthermore, research by Li et al. [15] suggests that the elevated levels of IL-6 and TNF-α in COPD patients with concurrent tuberculosis may exacerbate the breakdown of the extracellular matrix, stimulate the formation of fibroblasts, and induce airway remodeling. The ongoing inflammatory response may also result in abnormal structural and functional changes in the small airways and alveoli, causing lung damage. Consequently, the higher the levels of inflammatory factors, the more severe the symptoms and the poorer the lung function. This could be one of the mechanisms contributing to the greater lung function impairment observed in COPD patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis.

This study discovered that Patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis comorbidity demonstrated significantly higher PLT and plasma D-dimer levels compared to those with COPD alone. Platelets play a key role in inflammation and coagulation reactions, acting as a bridge between nonspecific and specific immune responses. After Mycobacterium tuberculosis invades the human body, the lipid and protein components it secretes activate neutrophils, leading to the release of substances such as histamine and prostaglandins, which in turn damage vascular endothelial cells. This destructive effect triggers an increase in platelet-activating factor (PAF) [16]. PAF not only promotes an increase in the number of platelets but also raises the proportion of large-volume platelets, which in turn increases the MPV and PDW. Elevated D-dimer levels also suggest that the body has secondary hyperfibrinolysis, often indicating the presence of thrombotic diseases. Previous clinical studies have also found that 3.9 % to 4.2 % of patients with pulmonary tuberculosis also have concurrent pulmonary embolism or venous thrombosis [17]. The results of this study suggest that the impact of tuberculosis infection on coagulation function is persistent, and therefore, patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis comorbidity exhibit a greater propensity for hypercoagulable states than those with COPD alone. Correlation analysis indicates that there is a certain correlation between the levels of inflammatory markers such as ESR and IL-6 and the levels of blood D-dimer, PLT, and FDP (P < 0.05). These findings suggest that coagulation abnormalities in patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis comorbidity may be associated with enhanced inflammatory responses, and those with heightened inflammatory responses tend to develop hypercoagulability. Therefore, clinicians should remain vigilant for elevated inflammatory markers and hypercoagulable states in this patient population.

This study discovered that patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis exhibited higher counts of peripheral blood lymphocytes compared to those with only COPD. However, research by Zhang et al. [18] also indicated that COPD patients with pulmonary tuberculosis had a decrease in natural killer (NK) cells and T lymphocyte counts. This reduction is attributed to the infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which can impair macrophage function, suppress lymphocyte proliferation [19], induce T lymphocyte apoptosis [20], and cause T cell exhaustion [21]. These factors may weaken the body's immune response to tuberculosis, thereby exacerbating the condition of COPD patients, although further in vitro experiments are needed to elucidate the specific mechanisms. The findings of this study suggest that the elevated lymphocyte levels in patients with stable pulmonary tuberculosis may be related to the fact that most observed cases were TB-IGRA weakly positive patients. Due to long-term activation of memory T lymphocytes caused by tuberculosis infection, these patients exhibited increased lymphocyte counts [22].

This study, being retrospective and with a limited number of cases, necessitates further validation of the effects of stable pulmonary tuberculosis infection on the inflammatory response and coagulation function in COPD through large-scale prospective studies.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study found that patients with COPD who had a stable pulmonary tuberculosis exhibited a stronger inflammatory response, which not only exacerbated lung function impairment but also induced a hypercoagulable state in the blood, however, whether tuberculosis infection increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (particularly pulmonary embolism) still requires incorporation of more relevant biomarkers and validation through large-scale studies. The findings of this study provide scientific evidence for understanding the pathogenic mechanisms by which stable pulmonary tuberculosis exacerbates chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), while also establishing a scientific basis for developing personalized treatment strategies for patients with concurrent stable tuberculosis.
